title: Einstein's 'Wormhole' Isn't a Tunnel — It's a Time Mirror!
summary:
Imagine looking in a mirror and seeing time flow backward. That's closer to what Einstein and his friend Rosen really discovered in 1935. They weren't building a tunnel through space — they found a mathematical bridge linking two copies of our universe, where time runs in opposite directions. Cool, right?

Later, people started calling these bridges 'wormholes' and imagined zooming through them to distant stars. But the original idea was never about travel. Einstein and Rosen were trying to understand tiny particles near super-heavy objects like black holes. Their bridge was a way to keep the rules of quantum physics (which describes the very small) and gravity (which rules big things) from fighting.

Here's the weird part: the bridge acts like a mirror in spacetime. On one side, time moves forward like we experience. On the other, time flows backward from a mirrored position. It's like having two clocks ticking in opposite directions, but both are needed to describe the whole system.

Why does this matter? It could solve a famous puzzle called the black hole information paradox. In the 1970s, Stephen Hawking said black holes eventually disappear, taking all the information about what fell in with them. But quantum physics says information can't be destroyed. The new idea says information isn't lost — it just switches to the backward time direction and eventually comes back out. So nothing vanishes forever.

We can't see these bridges because they're too tiny and unstable. But the math tells us they're there, helping the universe stay consistent. Next time you hear 'wormhole,' think less 'space tunnel' and more 'time mirror' — a hidden reflection that keeps the cosmos ticking.
why_it_matters: This mind‑bending idea shows that the universe has hidden rules to keep information safe, like a secret mirror that never forgets anything — even if a black hole tries to swallow it.

background_read: Albert Einstein (one of the most famous scientists ever) and Nathan Rosen (his colleague) worked on this idea in 1935, long before space travel was real.
Many science fiction stories use wormholes as shortcuts across the universe, but real science shows they are strange math bridges, not tunnels.
Stephen Hawking (a famous physicist) later showed that black holes should slowly disappear, creating the mystery of where everything inside went.
Article_Structure: WHO: Einstein and Rosen, two scientists
WHAT: Discovered a mathematical bridge in spacetime that acts like a time mirror, not a travel tunnel
WHERE: In their 1935 equations describing tiny particles near black holes
WHY: To connect quantum physics and gravity, and to explain where information goes in black holes

perspectives.description: This discovery opens up a whole new way to think about time. If information can switch direction, maybe the universe is like a giant clock that never truly loses anything.
These time mirrors are so tiny and unstable that we'll never see them. It's interesting math, but it might not change our everyday lives or technology.
Learning that something as wild as a time mirror could be real makes science feel magical. It inspires kids to ask big questions and maybe become scientists.
